name: The Ancient Douglas Firs of Indian Canyon
age_estimate: around 400 years (arborist estimate for the largest of the three)

location.address: Indian Canyon Park, on the cliff edge overlooking Mystic Falls, near Chief Spokane Garry's last campsite; trailhead at approximately 4812 W. Canyon Drive, Spokane

access: Free, public city park with hiking trails (part of the larger Palisades Park area, per spokanehistorical.org, which independently confirms the park is public, 155.7 acres, with trails)
transport: West Spokane, Indian Canyon trailhead off W. Canyon Drive; car recommended, some city bus service to the West Hills area
story:
These firs are still standing because they were not worth cutting down. A Douglas fir whose trunk tapers sharply makes poor lumber, and the crews who took nearly all the old growth out of the hills around Spokane walked past three of them on the cliff edge above Mystic Falls.

The largest is around 400 years old. That figure comes from Jeff Perry, the City of Spokane's lead arborist, who told the Spokesman-Review in 2019 that he could get his arms around perhaps a third of the trunk, and that measuring it properly is not really possible, because the tree's roots are holding the edge of the cliff together. That is the best description of it anyone has written. It is not so much standing on the canyon rim as being the canyon rim.

Four centuries puts their germination in the early 1600s. Chief Spokane Garry's last campsite is a short walk from where they stand; he died in 1892, by which time these three were already more than two centuries old.

One caution. All of this rests on a single newspaper feature, although a named city arborist with his arms around the trunk is better evidence than most trees get. No girth has ever been published, and the pin marks the trailhead rather than the trees.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by where they stand: three Douglas firs together right on the cliff edge above Mystic Falls, the largest of them wide enough that a grown man's arms reach only about a third of the way round.

name: The State Champion White Willow of Finch Arboretum

location.address: John A. Finch Arboretum, Spokane, Washington

transport: West Spokane, off Sunset Highway; car or city bus
story:
The largest white willow in Washington started life as somebody's garden tree. A woman came to the Spokane parks department to tell them so: her family planted it more than ninety years ago, when the ground that is now the John A. Finch Arboretum was still houses rather than trees.

The houses went. The willow stayed, and it is now the state champion of its species, the biggest known white willow in Washington, on the word of Jeff Perry, the city's lead arborist.

It is also on borrowed time, and the city says so plainly. In 2019 Perry gave it roughly thirty more years before it starts to split and come down, which is how large willows usually go: not in one storm but in pieces, over years. That is the bargain with the species. White willow grows fast and soft and generous, puts on size quickly and does not do centuries the way an oak does, so a willow of championship size is a rarer thing to stand in front of than ninety years makes it sound.

Its history rests on one newspaper feature and one family's memory, which is thinner than most trees here carry. If you know who planted it, or anything about the houses that used to stand here, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, long and narrow and silver underneath, so the whole crown goes pale when the wind turns them over. It is the largest willow in the arboretum, and the largest of its kind in the state.

name: The First Dawn Redwoods of Finch Arboretum

location.address: John A. Finch Arboretum, Spokane, Washington

transport: West Spokane, off Sunset Highway; car or city bus
story:
Botanists knew this tree from fossils before they knew it was alive. Metasequoia was described from imprints in rock, and everyone assumed that was the end of it, until a living stand turned up in a valley in central China in 1943. A species filed under extinct was still quietly growing.

Seed went out to institutions around the world, and in the 1950s the John A. Finch Arboretum received three of the first dawn redwoods brought to North America. Two are still standing. At about seventy-five years old they are infants by redwood standards, and they are also most of the species' history on this continent.

What makes them worth the walk is visible without knowing any of it. Dawn redwood is a deciduous conifer, which is close to a contradiction: soft feathery needles all summer, rust orange in late autumn, then bare all winter while every evergreen around it carries on as normal. The trunks flute deeply as they age, with vertical channels running down between the branches.

The arboretum is free and sits in west Spokane. These two stand a short walk from the state champion willow, so it is one afternoon rather than two trips. Nobody has recorded a girth for either of them; if you have a tape measure, we would take the number.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them in late autumn, when their needles turn rust orange and fall while the pines and firs around them stay green. In summer, look for soft feathery foliage on straight trunks deeply grooved between the branches.

best_time.label: late October into November, when two conifers in an arboretum of evergreens turn rust orange and go bare
